PREFACE

If one reflects carefully with a keen intellect, one finds that there is no instrument for attaining the four aims of life (dharma, artha, kama, and moksha — righteousness, wealth, desire, and liberation) other than the body itself; the body alone is that instrument. But it fulfills its functions properly only when it is free from mental and physical afflictions. Therefore it is proper to protect it in every possible way. For this very reason it is stated even in the texts on statecraft: "One should always protect the self, even at the cost of one's home, even at the cost of one's wealth." And the Lord Dhanvantari himself took incarnation for the protection of the body alone, and revealed Ayurveda — that Ayurveda whose Charaka Samhita was composed by the sage Charaka, through which he considered himself to have fulfilled his soul's purpose before the great sages. However, because it was composed by a great sage and is consequently difficult, the physicians of the present time have been unable to derive benefit from it. Therefore, having had a vernacular commentary prepared under the guidance of the learned Pandit Mihirachandra ji, we have carefully printed and published this universally useful work at our own "Shri Venkateswara" press. In its various sections, various subjects are described such that a physician who reads them has no need of other texts. And indeed, without Charaka, can a physician become proficient even by studying a hundred other works? It has also been said: "He who has not read Charaka — what kind of physician is he? He is but a servant of Yama (the god of death)." There is nothing more to say — can the water of the ocean fit inside a pot? That will be understood only by seeing for oneself. Thus it is enough.

Seeking the grace of the learned —
Khemraj Shri Krishnadas,
Director, "Shri Venkateswara" Press — Mumbai.

An illustrative diagram of the intestines (bowels), showing the full form of the alimentary canal (Alimentary Canal) from the throat to the rectum.

[DIAGRAM WITH NUMBERED LABELS 1 through 22]

In this diagram, the mark numbered 1 through 2 indicates the alimentary canal, the Oesophagus. 4 is the Stomach. From 5 to 8 is the upper portion of the tract. 7 is the Jejunum and 8 is the Ileum — these three together are called the small intestines (Small Intestines). 9 is the lower portion of the large intestine — the Caecum; and 10 is the Ascending Colon, 11 is the Transverse Colon, and 12 is the Descending Colon. These are collectively called the large intestines (Large Intestines). 13 is called the Rectum. 14 and 15 are the two Kidneys. 16 is the urinary Bladder. 17 is the Liver. 18 is the Gall-bladder. 19 is the Spleen. And where the number 2 appears, that is the Trachea, the second airway of the throat. 20 and 21 are the two Lungs, and 22 is the Heart. "Ka" and "Ga" mark the two main [illegible] passages. And "Ga" indicates the anus and the excretory opening.

Eye Ball (Netra Mandala)

Eyelid (Palak)

In this diagram:
"Nya" — the first layer of the eye, that is, the white membrane (sclera).
"Ka" — the transparent portion.
"Rva" — the second layer of the eye wall, that is, the dark membrane (choroid).
"Ga" — the transparent portion beneath it.
"Gha" — the space that is always filled with fluid (aqueous humor).
"Nga" — the third layer, that is, the membrane bearing the pupil (iris).
"Cha" — the pupil, that is, the dark portion.
"Chha" — the crystalline lens, the fourth layer, that is, the glassy substance.
"Ja" — the fluid matter within the eye, that is, the place of the colored lens-like substance (vitreous humor).
"Jha" — the optic nerve, that is, the vein of sight.

Physicians versed in Ayurveda consider there to be four layers (membranes) in the eye, while Unani hakims count up to seven, and modern doctors recognize only three membranes.

Lateral View of the Skeleton

Lateral Diagram of the Bones.
( Bones. )

The principal support of the body rests upon the skeleton. From it alone arise the body's shape, firmness, and power of movement. Upon it depends the conduct of all bodily functions. The total count of bones in the body, according to medical opinion, is as follows: in the skull 8, in the face 14, above the neck 9, in the sides 26, in the chest 9, in the ribs 21, in the complete arms 64, in all the feet 62 — thus altogether these make 200. The teeth number 32, and in each ear there are three small bones, making altogether 238. Adding 8 cranial bones, the total comes to 246.

And according to Ayurvedic medical opinion:
In all four limbs (arms and legs) there are 120 bones, in the trunk 117, and above the neck 63 bones. All these together make 300. See the chapter on Bodily Locations, Chapter 5, the fifth.

Now we shall expound the chapter on long life.
What follows is the commentary on the chapter regarding long life:

Verse 1: Desiring long life, the sage Bharadvaja approached Indra — the lord of the immortals, the protector of those who seek his refuge, he who is revered and worshipped.

Commentary: That is, Bharadvaja, the great ascetic who longed for long life, regarding Indra — the lord of the gods and the protector of those who surrender to him — went to his presence. ॥ 1 ॥

Verse 2: Prajapati received the Ayurveda in its entirety exactly as it was proclaimed by Brahma, and thereafter transmitted it onward.

Commentary: Just as Brahma had declared the Ayurveda, Prajapati caused the Ashvini Kumaras to receive it in full, and then from them... ॥ 2 ॥

Verse 3: From the Ashvini Kumaras, the lord Shakra (Indra) alone received the Ayurveda, and therefore Bharadvaja, at the request of the sages, went to Shakra.

Commentary: The Ayurveda was received solely by the lord Shakra from the Ashvini Kumaras; hence, at the urging of the sages, Bharadvaja went to Indra's presence. ॥ 3 ॥

Verse 4: Diseases appeared as obstacles in the lives of embodied beings who were engaged in fasting, austerity, study, and the vow of celibacy.

Commentary: When diseases became obstacles even for those engaged in austerity, fasting, study, and the vow of celibacy, causing obstruction to their lives... ॥ 4 ॥

130. A physician who desires to advance in the virtues of his profession should not accept food, drink, or wealth from a patient afflicted with disease. Thus a wise and modest physician preserves the wealth of his qualities.

131. He should make every effort as though he were the giver of life to human beings. That medicine alone is truly appropriate which brings about recovery from disease.

132. And that physician is foremost among physicians who liberates patients from their diseases — for success is declared to come from the correct application of all procedures.

133. Success, fame, and all good qualities are declared to belong to the most excellent physician endowed with all virtues. Thus ends this section.

FOURTH CHAPTER

Now we shall explain the chapter called Shadvirechana-shataashritiya (Relating to the Six Hundred Purgatives).

Thus spoke Bhagavan Atreya:

Here indeed there are six hundred purgatives. The six bases of purgatives; five hundred decoctions (kashaya); the five sources of decoctions; the five types of decoction preparations; and fifty great decoction groups — this is the summary of this chapter.

[Commentary:] That is to say, there are six hundred purgatives by firm reckoning; six supports (ashraya) of purgatives; five hundred kashaya (decoctions); five origins of kashaya; five types of kashaya preparations; fifty mahakashaya (great decoctions) — this is the total content of this chapter. 1.

The juice extracted by pressing a substance in a press is called svarasa (fresh juice); the paste made from ground substances is called kalka (paste). [Verse 10]

A substance boiled in water over fire is called shrita (decoction) by physicians; a substance ground and kept immersed in water overnight [is another preparation]. [Verse 11]

The cold decoction obtained [by soaking] is called kashaya; that which is obtained by macerating the substance in hot water and pressing it out is called phanta (hot infusion). [Verse 12]

Each of these preparations is progressively stronger than the one before it. Therefore, the selection of the form of preparation depends upon the strength of the disease and the patient — hence not all preparations are used universally everywhere. We shall now explain the fifty mahakashayas (great groups of decoctions) that have been mentioned. [Verse 13]

And they are as follows: Jivaniya (life-promoting), Brinhania (nourishing), Lekhaniya (scraping/reducing), Bhedaniya (purgative), Sandhaniya (healing/uniting), and Dipaniya (digestive-stimulating) — these constitute the group of six kashayas. [Verse 14]

Now we shall explain the chapter called Matrashitiya (on the proper measure of food).
We now describe the Matrashitiya chapter.

Thus has the Venerable Atreya said:
This has been stated by the Blessed Atreya.
One should eat in proper measure. The measure of food depends upon the strength of one's digestive fire. The amount of food that one has eaten, when it does not disturb the bodily wind and digests at the proper time — that is the measure of one's proper food quantity.

(Page 38 of the Charaka Samhita)

One must know this: Among food substances, shali rice, shashtika rice, mudga (green gram), lava (quail), kapinjala (partridge), ena (antelope), shasha (hare), sharabha (a deer), shambara (deer) and similar items are by nature light, yet they still require consideration of proper measure (matra). Similarly, food substances like milk preparations, masha (black gram), aquatic and marshy meats, and other foods that are by nature heavy also require measure. Thus it is not without reason that heaviness and lightness are attributed to substances. Light substances are rich in the qualities of wind and fire, while heavy substances are rich in the qualities of earth and water (soma). Therefore, light substances, by virtue of their own qualities, are said to kindle the digestive fire (agni) and cause little harm even when consumed to satiation. Heavy substances, however, do not have the nature of kindling the digestive fire, and when consumed beyond measure in an unusual manner, even those used with satiation become vitiated, unless there is strength of digestive fire and exercise. This measure, which depends on the digestive fire and bodily strength, does not mean that the nature of the substance is irrelevant — for heavy substances, it is taught that one should eat only one-third to one-half of satiation. For light substances too, one should not consider it entirely beneficial to eat to full satiation with regard to the proper use of digestive fire, because with respect to measure —

Thus the measure that is determined in accordance with one's digestive capacity, when properly followed without disturbing one's natural constitution, promotes strength, complexion, happiness, and longevity for the person.

The Eighth Chapter.
Now we shall explain the chapter called Indriyopakramaniya (concerning the approach to the sense organs).
Thus spoke the blessed Atreya.

After this, the chapter called Indriyopakramaniya is described. The blessed Atreya has stated it thus:

Here indeed there are five sense organs, five substances of the sense organs, five seats of the sense organs, five objects of the sense organs, and five cognitions of the sense organs — this has been stated in the section on the sense organs. Some further say that the mind, known as sattva, is beyond the senses, and all the endowments of the soul are dependent on it, and all activities are subject to it. || 1 ||

In this world, it is certain that there are five sense organs; there are five substances of the sense organs; there are five seats of the sense organs; there are five objects of the sense organs; and there are five cognitions of the sense organs — this has been stated in the section on the sense organs. And some say that the mind, called sattva, is supersensory; all the soul's endowments are under its control, and all activities are under its control. || 1 ||

The mind is the witness and ground of the activities of the sense organs. Because of their engagement with their own objects, and due to deviation and distraction, there is a multiplicity of sattva in one person. Because of the combination of the qualities of rajas, tamas, and sattva, there is not a singular multiplicity — since what is multiple cannot function in one person at one moment among many. || 2 ||

The activities of the sense organs serve as the evidence (witness) of their operations. Due to the divisions of self-interest, sense-object engagement, resolve, and deviation, there exist many kinds of sattva in a single person. Through the combination of the qualities of rajas, tamas, and sattva, they are not truly multiple — because multiplicity cannot operate in one person at the same moment. || 2 ||

Therefore the activity of all the sense organs takes place across multiple times. Whatever quality continuously accompanies a person, that quality of sattva, the sages call his predominant sattva, by reason of its abundance and predisposition. || 3 ||

Therefore, the activity of all the sense organs occurs at different times. Whatever quality of sattva remains constant in a person, the sages, by reason of its predominance, call that his sattva quality. || 3 ||

The sense organs, led by the mind, become capable of grasping their objects. Of these, the eye and ear [the text continues on the next page]

Verse 4: The five sense organs are those pertaining to skin (touch), nose (smell), tongue (taste), eye (sight), and ear (hearing).

Verse 7: Again, the senses, their objects, the self — all arise from the conjunction of these with one another.

Verse 8: These groups of five are of two kinds: momentary and determinative. Mind, the object of mind, intellect, and soul — this is the aggregate of the qualities of spiritual substance. That which is called action grounded in substance, which is the cause of the arising and cessation of auspicious and inauspicious activity, is what is meant by action.

Commentary 8: These exist in two sets of five: momentary and determinative. Mind, the object of mind, intellect, and soul constitute the collection of qualities of spiritual substance. This very collection is the cause of the inclination toward and withdrawal from good and bad, and the action grounded in substance that is spoken of — that is what action means.

Verse 9: Among these, the five sense organs — knowable by inference, constituted by the aggregate of modifications of the five great elements — are specially taught thus: fire is predominant in the eye, space in the ear, earth in the nose, water in the tongue, and wind in the skin.

Commentary 9: Among those, the five sense organs, which are knowable by inference and are constituted by the aggregate of modifications of the five great elements — in these, fire is specially present in the eye, space in the ear, earth in the nose, water in the tongue, and wind in the skin.

Verse 10: Among these, whatever element a sense organ is constituted of, it pursues only the corresponding object of that element — this follows from the nature and pervasiveness of that element.

The Eleventh Chapter.
Now we shall explain the chapter called Trisreshaniya [the three desires]. Thus spoke the Lord Atreya:

Here in this world, a person whose resolve, intellect, courage, and vigor are unimpaired — after rightly examining what is beneficial both in this world and the next — should pursue three Eshanas (desires/quests). ॥ 1 ॥

These are: the desire for life (Praneshana), the desire for wealth (Dhaneshana), and the desire for the next world (Paralokeshana). Of these three desires, one should first address the desire for life —

Why is the abandonment of life the abandonment of everything? Its preservation — maintaining health for the healthy person, and diligent care for the sick person's recovery from disease — these two matters have been stated and will be stated further. Thus, following what has been prescribed, one who properly tends to the preservation of life attains long life. Thus the first Esana (desire/quest) has been explained. (2)

These three are: Praneshana (the desire for life), Dhaneshana (the desire for wealth), and Paralokeshana (the desire for the afterlife) — that is, the desire for life, wealth, and the next world. Among these three desires, one should first attend to the desire for life, because when life is abandoned, everything is abandoned. The preservation of that life consists in maintaining the health of the healthy person and the diligent treatment of the sick — both of these have been mentioned and will be mentioned again. By thus tending to life in the manner prescribed, one attains long life. The description of the first desire is now complete.

Now the second desire — for wealth — is stated: After life, one should seek wealth by every means, for there is no sin worse than this: that a person without means (equipment/resources) should attain long life. Therefore one should strive to acquire the means, and the ways of acquiring those means are explained here. (3)

These are: agriculture, animal husbandry, trade, service to kings, and whatever other occupations are regarded by good people as respectable livelihoods that sustain and nourish existence — one should undertake those. A person who lives thus engaged enjoys a long life. The second desire, Dhaneshana, has now been explained. (4)

Now regarding the third desire — for the next world (Paralokeshana): The doubt here is: "How shall we be after departing from here — will we reach those realms or not? From where does this doubt arise?" It is said: there are those who, taking only direct perception as authoritative and regarding the next birth as not directly perceptible, take refuge in atheism; and there are those who, on the basis of scriptural authority, accept rebirth —

( 86 )

And because of conflicting scriptural statements: some consider the parents to be the cause of birth, some consider one's own nature (svabhava), some consider the will of God, and others consider pure chance (yadriccha) as the cause of rebirth — hence there arises doubt. Therefore one should ask: does rebirth exist or not? A wise person should abandon the attitude of atheism and doubt, because what is directly perceptible is little, and what is imperceptible is vast — that which is known through scriptural testimony, inference, and reasoning. And those very sense organs by which things are perceived directly are themselves imperceptible. || 5 ||

Now, proceeding to the third inquiry — that concerning the afterlife — doubt arises here: after leaving this body, what will one become, or will one become nothing? Why does this doubt arise? It is said: some people accept only direct perception, because rebirth is beyond the senses; some, even among atheists, rely on the authority of scripture (shastra) and on distinctions in scriptural testimony and thus desire rebirth; some attribute birth to parents, some to inherent nature, some to the creation of God, and some to chance. From all this arises the doubt — does rebirth exist or not? A wise person should abandon the disposition of atheism and doubt, because direct perception is limited and what lies beyond direct perception is vast — known through scripture, inference, and reasoning.

What is directly perceived, and those very sense organs through which things are known directly — those sense organs themselves are imperceptible. || 5 ||

Because of things being too close, too far, obstructed, due to weakness of the sense organs, due to distraction of the mind, due to similarity of qualities, due to being overwhelmed, or due to extreme subtlety — even existing forms and such are not directly perceived. Therefore it is untested and unsound to say that only what is directly perceived exists and nothing else — and the scriptures also confirm this: such a position is opposed to reasoning. || 6 ||

And when something is extremely near, or extremely far, or when there is obstruction, weakness of the sense organs, inattention of the mind, similarity among objects (assimilation), suppression (being overpowered), or extreme subtlety — even forms that are actually present are not directly perceived. So you abandon proper examination and say only direct perception is valid and nothing else exists — but the scriptures too affirm that this cannot be the reason, as it is contrary to reasoned argument. || 6 ||

If the soul of the mother or of the father were to transmit itself into the offspring, it would transmit either entirely or in parts. || 7 ||

Why are children of the same mother and father unequal? Among those born alike, complexion, voice, form, character, intelligence, and fortune differ; and birth in noble or low families, servitude, prosperity, happiness, unhappiness, length of life, and inequality of lifespan — obtaining in this world the results of one's deeds, and not obtaining them — even without being taught, crying, suckling, laughing, breathing and similar activities arise spontaneously; and in ordinary actions there are special fruits — in some actions brilliance of intellect, in others its absence; remembrance of one's former birth, arrival into this world, and the affection or aversion felt upon seeing those who departed from here — from all this it is inferred that one's own performed deeds cannot be set aside or destroyed; what remains from the previous body is the karmic bond called daiva (fate), and its fruit is only this. It cannot be otherwise. In this way, from the fruit the seed is inferred, and from the seed the fruit. ॥27॥

And the logical argument (yukti) is this: from the combination of the six constituents (dhatus) birth in the womb occurs; from the conjunction of the doer and the instrument, the fruit of performed action results — there is no fruit of unperformed action, and no sprout without a seed. The fruit corresponds to the action; from one seed another's sprout does not arise — this is the logical proof. ॥28॥

Thus, through the four means of valid knowledge described above, rebirth (punarbhava) is established, and thereafter the gateways of dharma are to be described. ॥29॥

So it is: in attending upon the teacher, in study, in the observance of vows, in marriage rites, in the procreation of offspring, in the maintenance of servants, in honoring guests, in giving gifts, in meditation, in austerity, in freedom from envy — that is, in not seeing faults in the virtues of others — keeping body, speech, and mind unclouded; in the examination of the self through intellect and inner perception, and in mental composure — and whatever other actions of a similar kind there are among the good, which lead to heavenly existence, proper birth, and nourishment — one should undertake to perform them. Among the sense organs, the organ of touch is the most pervasive, because the faculty of touch is distributed throughout the body and pervades all the other sense organs. Now we shall explain the chapter called Vatakalakaliya (on the degrees of Vata). Thus spoke Bhagavan Atreya.

Regarding the knowledge of Vata and its degrees — making this the subject of discussion — the great sages, wishing to enquire of one another, assembled and asked: What are the qualities of Vata? What provokes it and what pacifies it? What are its specific functions? How does the mind, when unsettled, provoke or pacify it through the means of provoking and pacifying? And what does Vata, when aggravated, do — moving within and outside the body — to the bodily elements? (1)

The great sages, desirous of acquiring this knowledge, sat together and questioned one another: What are the qualities of Vāyu? What causes its aggravation? What are its pacifying factors? And this Vāyu, which exists in an unstable, unsteady (wavering) state — without being provoked or pacified — does it cause aggravation or does it bring peace? And when it moves through both animate and inanimate bodies, and when it is present within the body, what are its functions, and what are they outside the body? (1)

Thereupon Kuśa Sānkṛtyāyana spoke: Rukṣa (dry), Laghu (light), Śīta (cold), Dāruṇa (fierce/harsh), Khara (rough), and Viṣada (clear/non-slimy) — these six are the qualities of Vāyu. Having heard this, Kumāraśirā Bharadvāja then spoke. (2)

He said: Indeed, exactly as the Blessed One has stated, these are the qualities of Vāyu. It is by virtue of these very qualities, by these very intensities, by these very influences and functions, that Vāyu, according to its measure in the body, becomes aggravated — for the continuous practice of similar qualities is the cause of the increase of the bodily tissues (dhātus). (3)

And thus through the continuous practice of similar qualities in substance, quality, and action, Vāyu attains aggravation, because the practice of similar qualities is the very cause of the growth of the dhātus. (3)

Having heard that statement, Kāṅkṣāyana Vālhīkibhiṣak spoke: Exactly as the Blessed One has said, it is so — these very factors cause the aggravation of Vāyu, and those opposite to them cause its pacification, because the opposite of the aggravating factors is indeed the cause of the pacification of the dhātus. (4)

Having heard that statement, Baḍiśodhāmārga spoke: Exactly as the Blessed One has said — these are indeed the factors that both aggravate and pacify Vāyu. We shall explain how, when the body is in a certain condition, the aggravating and pacifying factors either provoke or calm it accordingly. The factors that aggravate Vāyu are those that produce dryness, lightness, coldness, harshness, roughness, and clarity in the body — and in bodies of such a constitution, Vāyu finds its dwelling...

It is said that Agnivesha, seated among the renowned Sankhyas together with Punarvasu, asked his doubts for the benefit of the world. ||1||

"What are the sources of the snehas (oleaginous substances), how many snehas are there, what are the individual qualities of each sneha, what is the appropriate time and anupana (vehicle) for each one, and what are the other considerations?" ||2||

"What are the doses, and for which snehas are which doses prescribed; which sneha is beneficial for whom; and which is the best for the process of snehana (oleation)?" ||3||

"Who are the snehya (those suited for oleation) and the non-snehya; what are the characteristics of the snigdha (unctuous) and atisnigdha (excessively unctuous); what is the result of drinking it first, and what is beneficial or harmful when digested?" ||4||

"What are the mridukoshtha (soft bowels) and kurakoshtha (hard bowels); what are the possible complications; what are the signs of successful oleation; and in accha (pure) oleation and in shodhana (cleansing therapy), which form of application of sneha is considered appropriate?" ||5||

"In which conditions are the various snehas to be applied; O Lord of boundless wisdom, I wish to know from you the proper knowledge of the science of sneha." ||6||

Then Punarvasu, who was capable of resolving that doubt, replied: "The sources of the snehas are of two kinds — sthavara (plant-origin) and jangama (animal-origin)." ||7||

"Among these, tila (sesame), piyala, abhishuka, vibhitaka (belleric myrobalan), chitrak, abhaya (haritaki/chebulic myrobalan), eranda (castor), madhuka, sarshapa (mustard), kusumbha, bilva, abraka, mulaka (radish), atasi (linseed), nikoca, akhrot (walnut), karanja, and sauhinjana — ||8||

These are the plant-origin (sthavara) sources of sneha. Similarly, animals of the jangama class — fish, deer, and birds — are also sources. Among their products, dadhi (curd), kshira (milk), ghrita (ghee), mamsa (meat), vasa (fat), sneha, and majja (marrow) are described accordingly." ||9||

Among all oils, sesame oil is supreme. For the purpose of strengthening and lubrication (oleation), it is the foremost; castor oil is the best for purgation. || 10 ||

[Commentary on verse 1:] Does it mean that a physician who wishes to administer emetic or purgative substances to a king, to someone bearing the title of king, or to another very wealthy person should collect all the necessary materials before the medicine is taken? From the Charaka Samhita.

When a calamity becomes manifest, even the buying and selling of medicines becomes difficult, and the timely stockpiling (collection) of medicines as appropriate is not easy. Saying this, Agnivesha spoke to Bhagavan Atreya: [Verse 1]

"O Bhagavan, should not a knowledgeable physician from the very beginning make arrangements in such a way that the medicine is certain to succeed when applied exclusively? For the accomplishment of all actions depends on proper application, and failure too arises from improper application. Whether one undertakes an action properly or improperly, success or failure follows as a rule — because without correct understanding, knowledge becomes equal to ignorance." [Verse 2]

The meaning: O Bhagavan, a learned physician should conduct treatment in such a way that the medicine will certainly succeed, because the accomplishment of all actions through proper application is desirable, and disease (mishap) arises from improper application. An action begun properly or improperly will by rule reach success or failure respectively, for knowledge without proper practice becomes equal to ignorance. [Verse 2 — commentary]

Then Bhagavan Atreya replied to him: "It is indeed possible for us, or for others equal to us, O Agnivesha, to make such arrangements that the medicine succeeds with certainty through proper application — and there is no one here who can adequately teach the excellence of that application, nor anyone capable of grasping and retaining what has been taught regarding this medicine in this manner." [Verse 3]

"Or, having heard and grasped it, one should apply it again accordingly. For the subtle distinctions of place, medicine, season, strength, body, diet, wholesomeness, mind, constitution, and age are very fine indeed." [Verse 4]

The meaning: After hearing and understanding, one is empowered to know and to apply — because the varying states of dosha (humor), medicine, place, time, strength, body, diet, wholesomeness, mind, constitution, and age are extremely subtle. [Verse 4 — commentary]

"These matters, even when carefully contemplated, are capable of confusing the intellect of a pure and highly intelligent person — how much more so the intellect of one of limited understanding?" [Verse 5]

The meaning: These things, even upon reflection, confuse the mind of a person of clear and great intelligence — how then would they not confuse the mind of one of lesser intelligence? [Verse 5 — commentary]

Eighteenth Chapter.
Now we shall explain the chapter on Trishopha (the three kinds of swelling/edema).
Thus spoke the revered Atreya:

Three kinds of swellings arise — those caused by vata, pitta, and kapha. These again are of two kinds: intrinsic (nija) and extrinsic/traumatic (agantu). Among the extrinsic ones, they are caused by cutting, piercing, lacerating, breaking, crushing, pounding, striking, binding, bandaging, stabbing, pressing, and similar injuries; or by contact with the juice, pulp, and inherent properties of plants such as bhallataka (marking-nut), certain flowers, fruits, acrid herbs, itching plants, shrubs, and creepers; or by sweating, creeping insects, urination involving toxic matter; or from the fangs and teeth of venomous and non-venomous creatures...

[Left column:]
...arising from nail-wounds, and swellings caused by poison, wind, and heat arising from contact — these arise. They are recognized by their own characteristic signs and symptoms. Those caused by external factors, when treated partially with wound-bandaging, mantras, medicinal pastes and plasters, fomentations, and other such measures, subside. But those of internal origin are properly resolved through the appropriate application of oleation, sudation, emesis, purgation, enema, and nasal therapies; or they may worsen through improper dietary combinations. Conditions such as vomiting, fainting, cough, asthma, diarrhea, wasting, pallor, fever, abdominal disorders, prolapse, fistula, and hemorrhoids arise from improper suppression. Also from conditions such as skin diseases, itching, and eruptions; or from suppression of the urges of semen, flatus, urine, and feces; or in one who is emaciated from fasting and skin disease — through sudden consumption of heavy, very salty, ground preparations, fruits, vegetables, radish, green herbs, honey, alcohol, coarse grains, aquatic and marshy foods, meat; from eating clay or unripe things in excess; from compression of the fetus, premature delivery, and from improper treatment of newborns — swellings arise. These are the general causes.

[Right column:]
Now, the specific causes are as follows: Wind (Vata), aggravated by cold, rough, light, poison, fasting, excessive exercise, throwing, and similar factors, overpowers the skin, flesh, blood, and other tissues and produces swelling. It subsides when the patient lies down. Its color is dusky or reddish; it is unsteady in nature, pulsating, rough, and coarse; the skin and hair become loose; there is a feeling of being pierced, pricked with needles, as if ants are crawling over it; it feels like sesame seeds are being scattered; there is tingling; it contracts and stretches — this is Vata-type swelling.

Pitta, aggravated by hot, sharp, pungent, alkaline, salty, stale food, fire, sun, and heat exposure, overpowers the skin, flesh, blood, and other tissues and produces swelling. It subsides when the patient lies down. It is blackish, yellowish, blue, or copper-colored in appearance; hot, soft, with copper-colored hair; there is burning, throbbing, a sensation of being smoked or steamed, sweating, and intolerance of hot touch — this is Pitta-type swelling.

Kapha, aggravated by heavy, sweet, cold, unctuous foods, excessive sleep, lack of exercise, and similar factors, overpowers the skin, flesh, blood, and other tissues and produces swelling. It is slow in onset and slow to subside...

It becomes so. The pallid-white appearance, unctuous, smooth, heavy, stable, sluggish, white-haired, cold-tolerant, whitish — this is the phlegm-type swelling. According to the combination of their respective causes and forms, swellings arising from two doshas are named after those doshas. Similarly, from the combination of causes of all three, there arises a single tri-doshic type. Thus there are these varieties. And further, there is just one swelling in terms of its general characteristic of elevation. (1)

Now, there are three types of swelling (shopha): those arising from wind (vata), bile (pitta), and phlegm (kapha). They are further of two kinds — intrinsic (nija) and extrinsic (agantuka). Among these, the extrinsic ones arise from cutting, splitting, scratching, breaking, scraping, pressing, striking, binding, wrapping, crushing, squeezing; or from the flowers, fruits, and juices of plants such as Bhilaya, Atmagupta, Ashruka, worms, Shruka, Ahita, leaf-creepers, tumors, and such contacts; or from the stings, teeth, horns, and claws of venomous and non-venomous creatures; or from contact with sea-poisons, wind, cold, and fire — these give rise to swellings. They are such that, when the signs produced by their own causes first appear, treatments opposite to those signs — such as binding, mantras,

application of medicinal pastes, exposure to breeze, cooling, and similar therapeutic measures — bring about relief. And those that are intrinsic — they manifest from improper use of oleation, sudation, emesis, purgation, retention enemas, unctuous enemas, and head-purgation; or from improper combination of treatments; or from vomiting, laziness, cholera, asthma, cough, diarrhea, wasting, anemia, fever, abdominal disorders, fistula-in-ano, hemorrhoids, extreme thirst, skin diseases such as kushtha, itching, eruptions; or from suppression of the urges of vomiting, sneezing (saliva), belching, semen, flatus, urine, and feces; or from skin diseases and fasting; or from consuming food and substances that are very heavy, sour, salty, made of ground grains, fruits, vegetables, sauces, curds, raw vegetables, wines, weak barley preparations, shami-grain, various other grains, and meat from marshy regions; or from excess salt consumption; from compression of the fetus, from miscarriage of an immature fetus, and from improper treatment of born children — from excess of doshas, swelling manifests. This is the general cause stated. The specific point here is: through cold, dry, light, and toxic agents, as well as exertion, fasting, wasting, and emaciation, the wind (vata) becomes aggravated and, scorning the skin, flesh, and blood, produces swelling. That swelling arises and subsides quickly; it is dark-red or natural in color; it is moving, pulsating, rough, hard-skinned, with bristling hairs — it is as if cutting, splitting, and pressing, with piercing sensations like needles, and with a tingling-

The swelling moves over it like ants (lice), contracts and expands like mustard-paste applied to the skin. This is called Vata-shopha (edematous swelling due to Vata). And when one eats foods that are hot, sharp, pungent, salty, or sour, or when digestion is impaired, or when one is excessively exposed to fire or sunlight, then Pitta becomes aggravated and overpowers the skin, muscle, and blood, producing swelling. This swelling rises and subsides quickly. It is black, yellow, blue, or copper-colored in appearance; it is warm, soft, tawny, copper-colored, and hairless in character. Sensations as if of burning, smoke, heat, perspiration, and pricking seem to arise within it, yet its touch is not hot. This is Pitta-type swelling. And when one is excessively sedentary, fond of sweets, cold things, excessive sleep, and avoids exercise, Kapha becomes aggravated and overpowers the skin, muscle, blood, etc., producing swelling. This swelling rises with difficulty and subsides slowly. It is pale-white in complexion, smooth, heavy, firm, and large. The hair-tips over it appear whitish; it can tolerate hot touch. This is Kapha-type swelling. Just as, through their own causes and combination of features, three types of swelling arise from two doshas together, so also from the simultaneous aggravation of all three doshas (sannipata), one sannipata-type swelling arises. In this way there are seven types in all. Through various combinations of these basic natures, two, three, four, or seven varieties of swelling are found. The Twenty-Third Chapter.

Now we shall explain the chapter on Santarpana (over-nourishment).

The following are the means of over-nourishment: unctuous, sweet, heavy, and slimy substances; new grain, new wine, and the meat of marshy and aquatic animals. || 1 ||

A person who satisfies himself with these — and with dairy products, jaggery-mixed foods, and flour-based preparations in excessive quantities — who is averse to physical activity, who sleeps during the day and is devoted to the comfort of bed and seat. || 2 ||

In such a person, diseases arising from over-nourishment occur: urinary disorders, itching, skin eruptions, urticaria, anemia, and fever. || 3 ||

Also skin diseases, disorders of undigested matter, difficulty in urination, loss of appetite, drowsiness, impotence, excessive obesity, laziness, and heaviness of the body. || 4 ||

Obstruction of the sense organs and channels, clouding of the intellect, drowsiness, and edema — these and other such diseases afflict one who does not treat them promptly. || 5 ||

Recommended treatments for these are: emesis, purgation, bloodletting, exercise, fasting, medicated smoking, and sudation. || 6 ||

Also, consuming haritaki (chebulic myrobalan) mixed with honey, regular use of rough/dry food, and powders and pastes declared to be destroyers of itching and skin eruptions. || 7 ||

In this matter, Sharaloma said: "This is not so, because the Atman cannot ever join itself with disease and suffering by means of itself, since the Atman is averse to suffering." || 8 ||

The mind, known as the satva (consciousness), when pervaded by the qualities of rajas and tamas, becomes the cause of the arising of the body and of its disorders. || 9 ||

Food in its essence: Food is of one meaning, but by further classification it is of two origins — plant (sthavara) and animal (jangama). It is again twofold according to its beneficial or harmful effects. Its fourfold use is through drinking, eating, chewing, and licking. By the six-fold distinction of taste (rasa), it becomes sixfold. Its twenty qualities are: heavy, light, cold, hot, unctuous, dry, slow, sharp, hard, liquid, soft, firm, clear, slimy, smooth, rough, subtle, gross, dense, and flowing. Due to the innumerable varieties arising from combinations of substances, processes, and their multiplicity, countless preparations become fit for use. The best and most wholesome, as well as the most unwholesome for human beings — all of these we shall explain properly. Thus, red rice (lohita shali) is the most wholesome and the best among the grain cereals.

Since there is no essential difference in meaning, food is of one kind; but because it is of plant origin or animal origin, it is of two kinds. According to whether it is more beneficial or more harmful, it is used in four ways — as a drink (pana), as a meal (ashana), as something to be eaten (bhakshya), or as something to be licked (lehya). Its taste is of six kinds, and by the distinctions of the six rasas (tastes) it has twenty qualities: heavy, light, cold, hot, unctuous, dry, slow, sharp, unstable — and also: sharp, soft, hard, clear, slimy, smooth, rough, subtle, gross, dense, liquid, and penetrating. From these distinctions, the variations of substances and their combinations are innumerable in their abundance. The particular parts of those substances that are most useful, and the conception of their predominance, arise from the individual constitution (prakriti) of persons. A proper account is now given of foods that are most beneficial and most harmful: Among the shuka grains (bearded cereals), lohitashali (the red variety of sathi rice) is supremely excellent as a wholesome food. The six tastes, originating from the five great elements, are counted and named accordingly. ॥ 53 ॥

The waters that arise from the atmosphere are indeed of a soma (lunar/cooling) nature; by natural constitution they are cool, light, and of subtle, imperceptible taste. Among those six tastes: sweet taste arises from the predominance of the soma (lunar) quality; sour arises from the predominance of earth and fire; salt arises from the predominance of water and fire; pungent arises from the predominance of air and fire; bitter arises from the predominance of air and ether; astringent arises from the predominance of air and earth. [132] That which is contrary to fire and to one's habitual practice is called Satmya-viruddha (incompatibility with one's constitution).

[136] For a person of soft bowel constitution, a heavy purgative medicine is likewise incompatible with the bowel. This is known as Kotha-viruddha (bowel incompatibility). Cool, pure, auspicious, heavy, clear, and light — these six qualities belong to water that is by nature divine; such water, when it falls, depends upon the vessel that receives it. (192)

In a white vessel water becomes slightly astringent; in a pale-colored vessel it becomes bitter; in a reddish-brown soil it becomes pungent; in a saline soil it becomes salty; from mountain streams it becomes pungent; and in black soil it becomes sweet. (193)

These six qualities of water residing in the earth have been described. Similarly, Indra-water, which is of indistinct taste, is cool by nature and is free from any specific desire. (194)

The water that falls from the sky, created by Indra, and is collected in the vessels described above — the wise call it Indra-water, foremost among waters and fit for kings to drink. (195)

The qualities of all water in each season have been described here. Water that is slightly astringent, sweet, very subtle, clear, and light — (196)

The best water of all is non-unctuous and non-causing-congestion. Rain-season water is heavy, causes congestion, is sweet and light. (197)

In the autumn season the water that falls is generally fine, light, and non-causing-congestion. Such water is suited to those who are delicate, unctuous, and heavy eaters. (198)

For such persons it is recommended in all modes of eating — chewing, swallowing, licking, and drinking. In the Hemanta (early winter) season, water is unctuous, promoting of virility and strength, beneficial and heavy. (199)

In Shishira (late winter) water is somewhat lighter, productive of phlegm and wind, astringent, sweet, dry, and auspicious [text continues on next page]

Kings, ministers, and delicate persons should especially collect water in the autumn season. (202)

232. Jaggery (guda) causes worms, promotes blood, fat, and flesh, and increases diseases in excess.

Jaggery, by virtue of its coolness, clarity, and sweetness, is the best among sugarcane products such as bamboo sugar and sugarcane, but in excess it promotes worms, blood impurities, fat, and flesh. || 232 ||

233. Kshudra-guda (raw jaggery) dried to one-fourth, one-third, or one-half of its original volume is progressively heavier; washed jaggery (dhaut guda) contains very little impurity.

When raw jaggery is reduced to four parts, three parts, or half by evaporation, it becomes progressively heavier; washed jaggery has very little impurity. || 233 ||

234. Beyond that, matsyandika (a semi-liquid sugar), khanda, and sharkara are increasingly pure; and the purer each of these is, the cooler it is accordingly.

Matsyandika (raw syrup/rab), khanda, and sharkara (refined sugar) are all very pure; the greater their purity, the greater their cooling quality. || 234 ||

235. Jaggery-derived sugars are aphrodisiac, beneficial for those who are wasted or wounded, and contain fat; while mixed sugar (sharkara) is astringent, sweet, cooling, and slightly bitter.

Jaggery sugar is aphrodisiac, beneficial for the emaciated and injured, and is unctuous. Sugar mixed with fine crystals is astringent, sweet, cooling, and slightly bitter. || 235 ||

236. Honey-sugar is dry, destroys diarrhea and stimulates digestion, and is a cutting agent; all sugars are especially commended in thirst, bleeding disorders, bile disorders, and burning sensations.

Honey-derived sugar is dry, destroys vomiting and diarrhea, and is a cutting agent. All sugars are excellent for thirst, bleeding, excess bile, and burning sensations. || 236 ||

237. The four types of honey are: makshika, bhramara, kshaudra, and pauttika. Of these, makshika is the best; bhramara in particular is the heaviest.

Makshika, bhramara, kshaudra, and pauttika are the four varieties of honey. Makshika is the finest among them; bhramara is especially heavy. || 237 ||

238. Makshika honey is the color of oil; bhramara is said to be white; kshaudra should be known as tawny (kapila/yellowish); and pauttika is the color of ghee.

That which has the color of oil is makshika; that which is white is called bhramara; that which is tawny (yellowish) is kshaudra; and that which has the color of ghee is pauttika. || 238 ||

(Page 274)

Fasting, purgation — for those who have undergone oleation therapy and are thirsty thereafter, gruel (manda) with digestive-stimulating and light properties sustains life. (247)

The gruel of parched rice (laja-manda) alleviates thirst and diarrhea, equalizes the bodily constituents (dhatus), is beneficial, kindles the digestive fire, and removes burning sensation and fainting. (248)

This well-prepared gruel of parched rice should be given to those with weak or irregular digestive fire, to children, the elderly, women, and delicate persons. It is well-tolerated even when one is hungry and thirsty, and in purified persons it eliminates waste matter. (249)

Cooked rice (odana) that has been well-washed, has had its excess starchy water drained off, been properly steamed, and thoroughly heated is light in quality. Roasted rice is desired in conditions involving gara (artificial poison) and kapha disorders. (250)

On the other hand, rice that has not been washed, whose starchy water has not been drained, that has been improperly steamed, and that is cold, becomes heavy. (251)

Rice cooked with meat, vegetables, fat, oil, ghee, marrow, or fruits is strength-giving, nourishing, pleasing to the heart, heavy, and promotes bulk in the body. (252)

Similarly, rice prepared in combination with black gram, sesame, milk, or green gram has the same qualities; and kulmashas (a preparation of half-cooked pulse) are heavy, dry, vata-promoting, and cause loosening of the stools. (253)

Certain steamed foods, soups, barley-preparations, and gruels — the physician should prescribe their heaviness or lightness to the patient according to the nature of the substance involved. (254)

Unprocessed and processed soups, thin and properly prepared meat-broths, sour and non-sour preparations — each successive one in this order becomes progressively heavier. (255)

Verse 1:

Verse 2:

In it, the food substance called Prasada (the nutritive portion) produces a waste product called Rasamala (the impurity of rasa), and from the waste products arise urine, sweat, feces, vata, pitta, and kapha; and also the ears, eyes, nose, mouth, hair follicles, reproductive organs, excreta, head-hair, beard, body hair, nails, and other bodily parts are produced. [Verse 8] When the revered Atreya had spoken thus, Agnivesha said to him: "Lord, we see that even people who consume food designated as wholesome fall ill, and likewise those who consume food designated as unwholesome sometimes appear free of disease. Seeing this, how can we know that the specific use of wholesome and unwholesome substances truly produces the specific forms of good and ill?"

[Verse 9] Then the revered Lord Atreya replied to him: "O Agnivesha, for those who consume unwholesome food, diseases are indeed produced. And it is not merely that by consuming wholesome food alone one becomes completely free from all fear of disease. For there exist other causes of disease apart from unwholesome diet. These are: untimely conduct, failure of the intellect (prajnaparadha), the natural effects of time, and the qualities of sound, touch, form, taste, and smell, as well as unsuitability. These causes of disease afflict even the person who consumes proper food in the right manner. That is why even those who follow wholesome diet are seen to be ill. For those who consume unwholesome diet, however, not all faulty practices necessarily produce the same degree of dosa; nor do all dosas have equal strength; nor are all bodies equally capable of withstanding disease. Indeed, that which is unwholesome becomes more intensely harmful through the combination of place, time, potency, and excessive use. And that same dosa, when compounded with incompatible treatment, deep-seated, originating from the seats of life-force, striking at vital points, may become most severe and rapidly manifesting."

Then the revered Atreya spoke to Agnivesha: "O Agnivesha! Those who make proper use of wholesome food do not suffer disease on account of that wholesome food, yet the fear of all diseases is not completely overcome merely by the use of wholesome food alone. This is because other disease-causing factors exist independently of diet — namely, time and its adverse turns, errors of intellect, natural transformation, sound, touch, form, taste, and smell. These, being unwholesome in their nature, and working through the improper use of the sense-objects, connect a person to misfortune. Thus even those who use wholesome food may be seen afflicted with disease, while those who use unwholesome food do not immediately suffer harm from every cause. Nor do all unwholesome things cause equal harm, nor are all faults of equal strength, nor are all bodies equally capable of bearing disease. That same unwholesome substance, when combined with the wrong place, time, association, potency, and quantity, becomes exceedingly unwholesome. And those same aggravated doshas, when opposing the proper line of treatment in deeply lodged conditions, become destructive to the vital seats (marmas) long established in the abodes of the life-force — extremely distressing and very swift in effect." Therefore, those who know Ayurveda should be regarded as those who expound the questions of the chapters of the tantra-sthana, sentence by sentence, meaning by meaning, and component by component. (14)

Here the question arises: how do statements from the tantra etc. come to be expounded sentence by sentence, meaning by meaning, and component by component? To this it is said: the entire tantra, when spoken in accordance with its proper place, becomes expressed sentence by sentence. When, with the intellect fully entering into the true nature of the meaning, it is expressed through speech endowed with statement of thesis, reason, example, application, and conclusion — speech comprehensible to the threefold type of student's intellect — it becomes expressed meaning by meaning. The difficult meanings that are fixed in the tantra, when expressed through their explanatory elaborations (deliberations), become expressed component by component. Now if the student were to raise this question: of the four Vedas — Rig, Sama, Yajur, and Atharva — which Veda do the Ayurvedic scholars expound? What is life? What is the reason for Ayurveda? Is this Ayurveda eternal or non-eternal? What are its limbs? By whom is it to be studied, and to what purpose? (15)

In this, the disciple asks how the sentences, meanings, and components of the tantra can be properly stated. To this it is replied: the tantra of the sages, fully according to tradition, is expressed also sentence by sentence; entering well into the true nature of the meaning through the intellect, and expressed through speech that contains thesis, reason, example, application, and conclusion, comprehensible to the three types of a student's understanding — it is also expressed meaning by meaning. The difficult meanings fixed in the tantra, expressed through their elaborations (reflections), are also expressed component by component. If the student then asks whether it is the Rig, Yajur, Sama —

Sutrasthana 1
(303)

Among the four Vedas named after Atharvana, which Veda do the knowers of Ayurveda call the Veda of Ayurveda? What is ayu (life/lifespan)? From what does Ayurveda derive? Is that Ayurveda eternal (sanatana) or non-eternal? What are its limbs? Who is eligible to study it, and for what purpose should it be studied? (Verse 15)

On this matter, when asked by a physician, among the four Vedas — Rig, Yajur, Sama, and Atharva — it is the Atharva Veda that is declared to be the soul-portion (atma-bhaga) of Ayurveda. Because the Atharva Veda, through its collection of svastika rites, ayana (abodes), bali offerings, auspicious rites, homa, regulations, prayaschitta (expiations), fasting, and mantras and so on, expounds medicine. And medicine is taught for the benefit of life (ayu); this teaching is called Ayurveda. Now, in this context, ayu means: consciousness, vital force, continuance of life, and that which sustains — all these are one meaning. That which makes known (vedayati) this ayu is called Ayurveda. How is it to be described? By its own characteristics: through happiness and unhappiness, through benefit and harm, through what is valid and invalid; and because it makes known those substances, qualities, and actions that are life-promoting (ayushya) and life-diminishing (anayushya) — for this reason too it is called Ayurveda. The life-promoting and life-diminishing substances, qualities, and actions will be expounded by this treatise alone. (Verse 16)

In the section on Arista (signs of death), after treating the characteristics of bodily constitution (prakriti), Ayurveda has prescribed the measure of lifespan (ayus). The purpose of this science is: for the healthy person, preservation of health; and for the sick person, alleviation of disease. This Ayurveda is declared to be eternal, because it is beginningless (anadi), self-established in its own intrinsic characteristics (svalakshana), and because the nature of all existents (bhavas) is permanently fixed. It is not the case that the lineage of life ever failed to exist, or that the lineage of growth ever failed to exist. The knower of life too is eternal. Happiness, suffering, substance, cause, and characteristic mark — all are beginningless. Yet it is through the association of successive elements that this body of knowledge is gathered and examined: this is the definition of Ayurveda. The pairs of opposites — heavy and light, cold and hot, unctuous and dry, and so on — bring about increase and decrease through their universal (samanya) and particular (visesha) qualities respectively. As it has been said: by habitual use of heavy substances there is increase (upachaya) of heavy qualities and decrease (apachaya) of light qualities; and similarly for the rest. This is the eternal nature of existents. The intrinsic characteristics of substances such as earth and so on are fixed; substances exist, and their qualities are both eternal and non-eternal. || 20 ||

Ayurveda does not arise from something that did not previously exist and then come into being.
