The great sage Atreya spoke thus:

Here, the terms hetu, nimitta, ayatana, karta, karana, pratyaya, samutthana, and nidana are all synonymous with one another. Of these, the causes are of three kinds: unwholesome contact of the senses with their objects, errors of judgment (prajnaparadha), and the effects of time and season (parinama). From these three kinds and their variants, diseases arise — whether they are of the nature of Vata, Pitta, or Kapha, or of the twofold kinds, namely Rajasa or Tamasa in character. Among these, the words roga, amaya, gada, atanka, yakshma, jvara, and vikara are all synonymous. Its comprehension is through the five means: nidana (causative factors), purvarupa (premonitory symptoms), linga (signs and symptoms), upashaya (therapeutic test), and samprapti (pathogenesis).

(Page 315 — Nidanasthana)

The term "nidana" means cause; "purvarupa" means the premonitory signs of a disease before it fully manifests; "laksana" means the manifest signs. The term "linga" refers to shape and form, "cihna" means marks, "samsthana" means configuration, and "vyanjana" means expression — all these are synonymous in this context. "Upashaya" means the use of medicines, foods, and regimens that are either directly contrary to the cause of disease or contrary in effect — their result is a sense of comfort or relief. "Samprapti" (pathogenesis), "jati" (category), and "agati" (mode of onset) are all synonymous terms for the process of disease; it is further analyzed by number, predominance, type, variation, strength, and time. "Number" refers to, for example, eight types of fever, five types of gulma (abdominal tumors), seven types of skin disorders, and so on. "Predominance" is determined by comparing the relative degree of the doshas involved — whichever of the two is more prominent is designated as such. "Type" means that diseases are of two kinds by origin — endogenous and exogenous — and of three kinds by doshic involvement; and of four kinds by curability — mild, severe, curable, and incurable. "Variation" (vikalpa) refers to the partial dominance of doshas when they are co-present. "Strength and time" refers to the fact that the strength of a disease is governed by the seasons, day and night cycles, and dietary habits. Therefore, a physician, with his faculties of reasoning and intellect unimpaired, should understand diseases properly in all their aspects. This is the summary of the Nidanasthana; it will be explained in greater detail further on.

First of all, we shall explain the eight diseases arising from the causes of envy, hatred, and anger, in order, beginning with their nidana (causative factors). And we shall similarly explain the general outline of their treatment, and thereafter describe each disease in detail in due order. (Section 1)

(Hindi commentary:) Here it is established that hetu, nimitta, ayatana, karta, karana, pratyaya, samutthana, and nidana are all synonymous — that is, they are all names for nidana. Nidana is of three kinds: unwholesome contact of the sense organs with their objects (asatmya-indriyartha-samyoga), intellectual error (prajnaparadha), and the effects of time (parinama). Correspondingly, diseases too are of three kinds: those of fiery (agneya), watery/lunar (saumya), and wind (vayavya) character. There are also two further types: rajasa and tamasa. Among these, the terms amaya, gada, atanka, yakshma, jvara, vikara, and roga are not different in meaning. Their understanding (knowledge) comes through nidana, purvarupa, linga, upashaya, and samprapti. Of these, nidana means the cause — as already stated. The premonitory sign of a disease before it manifests is purvarupa. The manifest symptom of a disease is linga. In this, linga, akrti, laksana, cihna, samsthana, vyanjana, and rupa are all not different in meaning. In this sense, upashaya is that which...

( 316 )

The medicines, diet, and regimen that are opposites of the disease and its causative factors, and their comfortable association — the terms "samprapti," "jati," and "agati" do not differ in meaning from one another. Through the distinctions of number, predominance, type, variation, strength, time, and specific form, the classification of diseases is determined — for example, eight types of fever, five types of gulma (abdominal tumors), seven types of kushtha (skin disorders), and so on. Predominance is understood through the lesser or greater presence of the doshas; this is called the "taratama bhava" (the principle of more or less). When comparing two, the suffix "tara" applies; when comparing three, "tama" applies. In this manner, diseases are of two kinds based on the distinction between intrinsic (nija) and extrinsic (agantuja) causes. From the distinction of the three doshas, three types are recognized; from the distinction of curable, incurable, mild, and severe, four types are recognized. The proportional variation in the combined doshas, and the specific quality of strength and time particular to each disease, are governed by the rules of season, day-night cycle, diet, and time. Therefore a physician who wishes to understand diseases correctly must know their causative factors and other characteristics truly. This is the summary of the Nidana Sthana (section on etiology). Its detailed explanation follows hereafter. Therein, beginning with the eight diseases that arise from greed, malice, and anger in the wealthy (adhya), they are described in order with their etiologies, and likewise the summary of therapeutic principles, the later course of treated patients, and the sequential description of the specified disorders are set forth. (Section 1)

Here, fever (jwara) is the first among diseases to be described. Among these, those of bodily origin come first. Now: from eight causes does fever arise in human beings — from vata, from pitta, from kapha, from vata-pitta combined, from pitta-kapha combined, from vata-kapha combined, from all three together (vata-pitta-kapha), and from external (agantuja) causes. We shall describe its etiological features, premonitory signs, characteristic symptoms, and stages of development. Furthermore, through excessive indulgence in rough, light, cold foods; excessive exercise, emesis, purgation, enema, nasal therapy; suppression of natural urges; fasting; physical injury; sexual excess; mental agitation, grief, excessive bleeding, wakefulness, uneven bodily postures — through all these, vata becomes aggravated. When that aggravated vata, combined with heat, enters the site of the digestive fire (amashaya), it obstructs the channels carrying the essence of food, the tissues, and their nourishment, and disrupts the digestive fire at its seat, driving away the body's heat — then fever is produced. Its characteristic signs are: irregular onset, heaviness of the body, and variation in the distribution of heat throughout the body...

(Page 317 — Nidanasthana, Chapter on Fever/Jwara)

[Left column:]
The manifestations and stages of fever (jwara): toward the end of digestion, at the end of the day, and at the end of sweating, there is aggravation or onset of fever. Its special signs include roughness and redness of color in the nails, eyes, face, urine, feces, and skin; an excessive sense of heaviness; various pains in the limbs, moving and unsteady. In the calves there is cramping; in the knees, a feeling of separation of the joints; in the thighs, weakness; in the waist, sides, back, shoulders, arms, and chest, pain as if broken, crushed, or bruised; a ringing or rattling sound in the ears and temples; an astringent taste in the mouth; a disagreeable taste; dryness of the palate and throat; thirst; a gripping sensation in the heart; dry retching; dry cough; sneezing; inability to retain things; perspiration; loss of taste and appetite; indigestion; despondency; yawning; trembling; delirium; insomnia; horripilation; sensitivity of the teeth — all these arise. Furthermore, there is no proper nourishment from the causes prescribed (for health), but instead their opposite — excessive nourishment from what is contrary. These are the signs of vata-fever. Sour, salty, pungent, undigested foods —

[Right column:]
— when excessively consumed, as well as excessive sharp heat, exertion, anger, and irregular diet: by these pitta becomes aggravated. Then the aggravated pitta, starting from the amashaya (stomach), heats up the digestive fire; blocking the channels that carry the essence of food — rasa, sweat, and the like — with obstructions, it overwhelms the sites of digestion and drives the heat out through the openings, heating the entire body alone, and thus produces fever. Its signs are as follows: the fever comes on and intensifies simultaneously throughout the whole body. In one who has eaten, especially at midday and afternoon, there is a burning sensation, bitterness of the mouth, inflammation of the nose, mouth, throat, and lips, thirst, dizziness, intoxication, fainting, vomiting, diarrhea, aversion to food, exhaustion, perspiration, skin eruptions (kotha), yellowish or greenish discoloration of the body, nails, eyes, face, urine, feces, and skin, an intensely hot feeling, and excessive burning heat. The prescribed causes showing no nourishment but their opposites showing increase — these are the signs of pitta-fever. [Next: signs related to cold, heavy, unctuous, sweet —]

(Page 318 of the Charaka Samhita)

Excessive indulgence in slimy, sour, and salty foods, daytime sleeping, excitement, and physical exercise leads to aggravation of kapha (phlegm). When this aggravated kapha enters the stomach, it mixes with the digestive heat, pervades throughout the nutrient essence of digested food, blocks the channels, suppresses the digestive fire, either drives the heat away from its seat of digestion or expels it outward, and by pressing down on the body alone, it produces fever. These are its signs: simultaneous onset of fever throughout the body, a sense of heaviness, nausea, loss of appetite, increased salivation, sweetness in the mouth, cold sensation, drowsiness, cough, pain in the heart region, heaviness of the eyes, excessive sleep, stiffness, drowsiness, labored breathing, cough, sneezing, coldness, pallor of the eyes, nails, face, urine and skin, excessive cold sensation, eruptions on the limbs, and non-increase of the stated causative factors or their contrary increase — these are the signs of kapha-fever.

From irregular eating, fasting, non-evacuation of the bowels, unwholesome smells inhaled, drinking water hated by the patient, contact with trees of the forest, improper use of emesis, purgation, enemas, head-cleansing therapies, from intercourse with women of forbidden categories, from wrong treatment of the named conditions, and from the combination of the stated causes — from any one of these, or from all three doshas simultaneously becoming aggravated, they then produce fever one after another in due order. By observing the mixed appearance of the signs of the fevers described, one should recognize a particular fever as dual-doshic or sannipata (triple-doshic). The eighth type of fever arises from external causes — from physical injury, demonic affliction, black magic, and curses. For some time it remains as a purely exogenous fever, but afterward it becomes bound to the doshas. The one caused by injury is associated with vitiated blood through the agency of vata; the one caused by demonic affliction is bound by both vata and pitta; those caused by black magic and cursing are bound by sannipata. Since this fever is distinguished from the other seven fevers by its characteristic signs, mode of treatment, and manner of arising, it is to be recognized as distinct.

Page 319 — Nidanasthana (Section on Etiology)

These should be understood through common features of action. Fever (jvara) is thus described as having eight varieties of constitutions. Fever has heat (santapa) as its single characteristic mark; it is described in two ways according to a particular intention — as intrinsic (nija) and extrinsic (agantu). Among these, the intrinsic is described as twofold, threefold, fourfold, and sevenfold, according to the variants beginning with Vata. These are the prodromal signs: bitterness of mouth, heaviness of the limbs, loss of desire for food, disturbance of vision, excess of sleep, restlessness, yawning, trembling, exhaustion, delirium, wakefulness, horripilation, intolerance of sound, music, wind and sun, loss of appetite, indigestion, debility, pain in the limbs, lassitude, loosening of the body, long-windedness, idleness, diminution of work previously undertaken, aversion toward one's own duties, irritability toward teachers' words, hostility toward children, indifference to one's own dharma, aversion to thinking of garlands, ointments, food, and hair-care, aversion to sweets and pleasures, and craving for salt and pungent things — these are the prodromal signs of fever. Because these, beginning with heat, accompany and follow the state of fever and afflict the sufferer, these are the individual symptoms of each type of fever, described in full or in brief.

Fever, verily, arises from the wrath of Maheshvara; it destroys the life-force of all beings; it afflicts the body, senses and mind; it destroys strength, color, joy, enthusiasm; it causes exhaustion, delusion, and suppression of appetite; it burns the bodies — thus is fever. No other disease is as fierce, causing so many complications and so difficult to treat. Fever is the lord of all diseases; it is described by many names in the various forms of life. All living beings are born with fever and die with fever; being overwhelmed by it, they lose their memory of all past deeds; fever alone takes away the life-breath from all creatures.

For one who shows prodromal signs of fever, light food and non-nourishing diet should be prescribed at the outset, since fever arises from the stomach (amashaya). Then, decoctions of astringent herbs, massage, sudation, poultices, ointments, emesis, purgation, enema, anuvasana enema, nasal treatments, medicated smoking, collyrium, and milk-diet should be administered as appropriate. In all cases of chronic (jirna) fever, intake of ghee is recommended. Medicated ghee prepared with appropriate herbs destroys by its processing the kapha and cold that have accumulated, and restores the bodily heat; therefore, in cases of chronic fever —

( 320 )

"In all [substances] that have been combined with water and immersed [in liquid], these [properties apply]." — [Verse] 2

Now, fever (jvara) is spoken of first among all bodily disorders. Being the foremost among the diseases of the body, it arises in human beings from eight causes: from vata (wind), from pitta (bile), from kapha (phlegm), from vata-pitta combined, from pitta-kapha combined, from vata-kapha combined, from vata-pitta-kapha combined, and the eighth cause being external (agantuja). The text proceeds to teach the specific nidana (causative factors), purvarupa (premonitory signs), linga (symptoms), and upachaya (aggravating conditions) of that fever.

The excessive use of the following leads to provocation of vata (wind): rough, light, and cold [foods or substances], exercise, vomiting, purgation, retention enemas, nasal therapies, excessive suppression of natural urges, fasting, physical injury, sexual activity, anxiety, grief, hemorrhage, excessive wakefulness, irregular posture of the body. When provoked, that vata enters the stomach (amashaya), mingles with the bodily heat (ushma), and following the first product of food-digestion known as rasa-dhatu (nutritive fluid), it blocks the channels (srotas) through which rasa and sweat flow. It then drives the heat out of the site of digestion into the body alone, and thus produces fever.

The signs of this [vata] fever are as follows: irregular onset and cessation, unevenness of bodily heat, extreme instability [of temperature], arising and increasing at the end of digestion, at the end of the day, or at the end of perspiration. The fever is characteristically rough and reddish; the nails, eyes, mouth, urine, feces, and skin become discolored. There are many kinds of moving and stationary pains; the knees and joints of various limbs tremble; the thighs feel numb; the loins, flanks, back, shoulders, arms, shoulder-joints, and chest feel as though broken, diseased, crushed, churned, pressed, or struck. The jaw becomes stiff; there is ringing in the ears and continuous shooting pain in the temples; the mouth tastes astringent and unpleasant; the mouth, palate, and throat become dry; there is intense thirst, great dryness in the heart region, cough, sneezing, suppression of belching, distress over the taste of food, excessive salivation, anorexia, indigestion, depression, yawning, fatigue, trembling, exhaustion, delirium, sleeplessness, horripilation, and sensitiveness of the teeth. Likewise, whatever is stated in the nidana as being agreeable (priti) to heat, its diminution — and the increase of its opposites — all these are the signs of vata-fever.

Excessive consumption of hot, sour, salty, alkaline, and pungent foods, as well as of undigested food, and similarly, exposure to intense sunlight, heat from fire, exertion, anger, and irregular eating — these provoke pitta (bile). When provoked, pitta — arising from the stomach itself — mingles with the bodily heat, combines with rasa (the first dhatu, the nutritive fluid that is the product of digested food), blocks the channels carrying rasa and sweat, impairs the digestive fire through its own liquid nature, and afflicting the heat outside the site of digestion, reaches the body alone — [the text continues on the next page].

When it occurs, it produces fever. Its signs are as follows: the onset or increase of fever in the body happens only once at a time — during the period of digestion of food, at midday, at midnight, at the beginning of the day, or especially in autumn. In the mouth there is bitterness; the throat, lips, and palate feel as if burning; there is thirst, fainting, confusion, loss of consciousness; there is bile-induced purging; aversion to food; exhaustion; perspiration; delirium; eruption of reddish patches on the skin; yellowish-green and golden discoloration of the nails, eyes, mouth, urine, feces, and skin; intense burning heat; and in cold conditions a sensation of internal heat. In the etiology, a decrease of the factors mentioned and an increase of their opposites — these are the signs of pitta-fever.

Oily, sweet, heavy, cold, slimy, sour, and salty substances; sleeping during the day; excessive joy; excessive exercise — when these are used excessively, kapha becomes aggravated. When it becomes aggravated, it enters the stomach, mingles with heat, follows the nutrient substance (rasa) which is the transformation of previously consumed food, and covers the channels that carry rasa and sweat, suppresses the digestive fire, and drives the heat out of its seat of digestion. Afflicting the body heat, it reaches the body alone and then produces fever. Its signs are: the onset or increase of fever in the body occurs only once; it especially occurs immediately after eating, in the forenoon, or in spring. Heaviness of the limbs, absence of desire for food, salivation, sweetness in the mouth, nausea, a coating over the heart, sluggishness, excess of sleep, stiffness, drowsiness, dyspnea, cough, catarrh, chilliness, whitish discoloration, and cold sensation in the eyes, nails, mouth, urine, feces, and skin — an intense cold arising from the limbs, while in warmth there is a drawing sensation — and in the etiology, a decrease of those mentioned and increase of their opposites — these are the signs of kapha-fever.

For those who eat irregularly, through fasting, through change of food, through the influence of the season, through smelling of unwholesome odors, through use of water contaminated by poison, through contact with venomous creatures, through association with mountains, through improper use of oleation, sudation, emesis, purgation, enema (āsthāpana and anuvāsana), and nasal therapy, through improper use of these, and through abnormal childbirth in women, and through improper care of mothers after delivery, and through the mixing of the causes mentioned — according to the learned, in dual combinations (dvandva), one or all three doshas together may become simultaneously aggravated. Being aggravated, they produce fever in the same sequence described above. In that fever, by the characteristic mixing of the fever signs as described, one should recognize either a dual-dosha (dvandvaja) or triple-dosha (sannipātaja) fever.

From physical injury (abhighāta), from demonic possession (abhiṣaṅga), from sorcery (abhicāra), and from cursing (abhiśāpa) — from these arises the eighth type, the exogenous fever (āgantu-jvara), in the manner described above. This exogenous fever exists for some time as an independent condition and then becomes associated with the doshas. The abhighāta-type is seated in the blood and is associated with vāyu, and the abhiṣaṅga-type is associated with vāta and pitta.

( 322 )

Amishapaja (fever born of meat/flesh causes) and Abhicharaja (fever born of black magic/ritual harm) — these two combine with Sannipataja (triple-dosha) fever. The specific signs arising from the treatment approaches of the seven types of fever being present, this is to be understood as Agantuja (exogenous) fever. Through ordinary karmic means, the nature of these eight types of fever has been described. Fever has only one characteristic: heat. By distinction of intent and by distinction of the intrinsic and exogenous types, it is spoken of in two ways. Among those described variously as being of two, three, four, or seven types based on Vata and the other doshas, their prodromal signs are as follows: a bad taste in the mouth, heaviness in the limbs, loss of appetite, restlessness in the eyes, the coming of tears, excessive sleep, frequent yawning, bending of the body, trembling, exhaustion, dizziness, delirium, wakefulness, horripilation; inability to bear sound, song, wind, or sunlight; loss of taste, indigestion, weakness, pain in the limbs, lassitude, diminishment of vital breath; procrastination, laziness, decline even in accumulated duties, a contrary intellect in one's own affairs, contempt for the words of elders, aversion toward children, neglect of one's own dharma, indifference toward garlands, ointments, and food; aversion to hair-care and sweet substances, fondness for sour, salty, and pungent things — all these are the prodromal signs of fever. Even before the heat appears, these bind the afflicted person with distress. Thus these are the individual signs of each fever. To speak briefly and at length: fever surely arises from the wrath of Mahadeva (Shiva). It is the destroyer of the vital breath of all living beings. It is the cause of burning in the body, senses, and mind. It suppresses marrow, strength, complexion, joy, enthusiasm, and causes weakness, exhaustion, fatigue, stupor, and obstruction of food. That which causes the body to age (jara) is called Jvara (fever). No other disease is as terrible, as troublesome in its complications, or as difficult to treat as this fever. It is the lord of all diseases, spoken of by many names in various kinds of existence. All living beings are born with fever and die with fever. That fever is the great delusion; those embodied beings overpowered by it do not remember even a little of the karma of their previous body. Fever takes all living beings; therefore, upon seeing its prodromal signs or at the onset of fever, one should reduce food intake, since fever originates in the stomach (amashaya). Thereafter one should use: decoction-drinking, oil massage, sudation, application of pastes, affusion (pouring water), mild purgation, enema, anuvasana (oil enema), pacifying therapies, nasal administration (snuffing), fumigation, smoke inhalation, collyrium (eye application), and consumption of milk. With appropriate measures and reasoning, in all cases of chronic fever (jirna jvara), the drinking of ghee prepared with suitable medicinal herbs is considered the best, because ghee by its natural quality pacifies Vata, by its processing pacifies Kapha, and by its coolness pacifies Pitta and heat. Therefore, in all chronic fevers, ghee is as beneficial and excellent as water is to things burned by fire. || 2 ||

Second Chapter.
Diagnosis of Raktapitta (hemorrhagic disorder).
Now we shall explain the diagnosis of raktapitta.

Thus indeed spoke the Blessed Atreya.
Next follows the diagnosis of raktapitta (hemorrhagic disorder).

(Page 324)

The revered Atreya explains and states as follows:

Pitta, as it truly is, comes to be known by the designation "lohita-pitta" (blood-bile); that same pitta will now be described accordingly. When a living being habitually and ignorantly consumes foods that are predominantly of the yavaka, uddala, koraka, and dushaka varieties — and also frequently eats other foods that are excessively hot and sharp — along with dishes prepared with nishpava (a type of bean), masha (black gram), kulattha (horse gram), and alkaline soups; with condiments such as digha, manda, mathha, sour and pungent preparations, and various kinds of kanji; along with the flesh of boar, buffalo, sheep, fish, and cow, mixed with the vegetable preparation of pindalaka; with radish, mustard, garlic, karanja, shigru (drumstick), shimbhu (a legume), khadayusha, bhustrina, and similar items; with surasa, kathera, kandira, kalaka, phanasa, kshavaka, and phanijjaka as side-dishes; with sura (fermented drink), sauvira, tushodaka, maireya, mechaka, madhulaka, kuvala (jujube), and badara (Indian plum) with sour substances as the principal accompaniments; and after consuming such starchy foods, drinks excessively while tormented by intense thirst, and repeatedly or in large quantities takes milk together with such foods; when the flesh of rohini, kala, and kapota birds is cooked in mustard oil with alkali, and one eats it together with sour fermented preparations cooked with kulattha, masha, pinyaka, jambu, and likucha, and then drinks raw milk repeatedly or drinks it while extremely heated — when a person behaves in all these ways, his pitta becomes aggravated and his blood (lohita) exceeds its normal measure. ॥ 1 ॥

When pitta, thus excessively increased beyond its proper measure and provoked, spreads throughout the body, it clearly manifests its influence upon the channels (srotas) that carry blood (lohita)...

(Page 325)

Verse 2:
When blood flows heavily from the mouth along with excess discharge, it corrupts that very blood.

When it exceeds the normal measure, the aggravated pitta, spreading through the body, reaches the channels (srotas) that carry blood originating in the liver and spleen, and by causing excess discharge (abhishyanda) and heaviness in the openings of those channels, it corrupts the blood itself. (2)

Verse 3:
By corrupting the blood internally through association, and by causing the blood to take on the smell and color of pitta, pitta is also called "lohita" (blood). (3)

The prodromal symptoms (purvarupas) of this condition are as follows: loss of desire for food; burning sensation after belching; repeated vomiting with a sour, fermented smell; fear after vomiting; change of voice; exhaustion of the limbs; burning sensation; smoke-like sensation rising from the mouth; a raw smell resembling iron, blood, and fish; the blood, urine, sweat, saliva, nasal secretions, ear wax, and bodily waste turning greenish-yellow like turmeric; formation of lumps and pustules on the body; pain and sensation in the limbs; and repeatedly seeing in dreams visions of red, blue, yellow, dark, and luminous forms — these are the prodromal signs of raktapitta (hemorrhagic disorder). (4)

Verse 5:
The complications (upadravas) are certainly these: weakness, loss of appetite, impaired digestion, dyspnea, cough, fever, diarrhea, edema, emaciation, pallor (pandu disease), and hoarseness of voice. (5)

The two pathways of this disease are upward and downward. The upward path: when associated with kapha in the body, the blood is discharged upward through the ears, nose, eyes, and mouth. When vata predominates in the body, through association with vata, it moves downward and is discharged through urine and feces...

(Page 326)

It flows through the channels. When there is excessive kapha and vata mingling in the body, it flows out through the upper passages. Thus, in those with excessive kapha, due to the combination of kapha with vata in the upper region, it drips from the ears, nose, eyes, and mouth. When vata predominates, that kapha, having reached the lower regions of the body through the combination of kapha and vata, flows out through the urinary and fecal passages. When vata and kapha combine together, it reaches both passages, and whatever accumulates in both passages flows out through all the orifices mentioned earlier. (Verse 6)

Of these, that which is in the upper portion of the body is curable, because treatment by purgation is applicable and many medicines are available. (7)

That which falls into both portions is incurable, because neither emesis nor purgation is applicable to it and no medicine exists for it. (Verse 9)

The aggravation of raktapitta (hemorrhagic disorder) certainly arose in the past at the time of the destruction of Daksha's sacrifice, through the wrath and indignation of Rudra, when the life-forces had departed from the bodies of living beings, and it arose in them following fever. (Verse 10)

For this rapidly acting, life-threatening condition, like a forest fire, one must quickly strive for its pacification. Having carefully examined the dose, site, and time, one should treat it either by nourishing (santarpana) or by reducing (apatarpana) therapy, using soft, sweet, cooling, bitter, and astringent foods and drinks, and through applications, douches, immersions, and therapeutic touch, and also through emesis and other methods, being careful and diligent in all the prescribed measures. That which is extremely foul-smelling, excessive in quantity, accompanied by all complications, and which causes destruction of strength and flesh — that raktapitta is also incurable, without hope of remedy. (23)

The person afflicted by raktapitta who sees visible objects or the sky as red — that too is certainly incurable, without doubt. (24)

Among these: the incurable should be abandoned; the manageable (yapya) should be carefully maintained; and the curable (sadhya) should be treated by an attentive physician using well-established medicines. (25)

There are two verses on this subject: the causes, premonitory signs (purvarupa), complications, the two pathways (channels), the binding of the doshas, treatability, and the causal factors — all these are to be known. (26)

Punarvasu, free from delusion, the fault of passion, greed, arrogance, pride, and longing, thus expounded the etiology of raktapitta. (27)

Thus ends the second chapter, named "The Etiology of Raktapitta," composed by Agnivesha and revised by Charaka.

In sum: in the etiology of raktapitta, Punarvasu — free from delusion, the blemish of rajas, greed, vanity, intoxication, and desire — has given this exposition. (27)
Thus ends the summary of the etiology of raktapitta. Chapter 2.

(329)

Third Chapter.
Now we shall explain the diagnosis of gulma (abdominal tumors/swellings).
Thus spoke the revered Atreya.
After this, the description of gulma-nidana is given; the revered Atreya says thus—

Here indeed five gulmas arise, namely: vata-gulma, pitta-gulma, shlesma-gulma, nichaya-gulma, and shonita-gulma. (1)

Here it is certain that there are five gulmas, which are: vata-gulma, pitta-gulma, shleshma-gulma, nichaya-gulma, and shonita-gulma. (1)

To the revered Atreya speaking thus, Agnivesha said: "O Revered One, how may we distinguish among these five gulmas here? For even a physician who knows medicines but does not know the specific distinctions of diseases is incapable of curing them." (2)

In this manner, Agnivesha spoke to the revered Atreya: "O Lord, how shall we recognize the distinguishing features of each of the five gulmas? One who does not know the specific nature of diseases — even if he knows medicines — is incapable of curing those diseases." (2)

To him spoke the revered Atreya: "O Agnivesha, the specific knowledge of gulmas and other diseases comes from their origin, premonitory symptoms, signs, sensations, and responses to treatment. Now listen carefully to what is said regarding gulmas." (3)

When a person of vata constitution, especially weakened by one of the following — fever, vomiting, purgation, or diarrhea — or by emaciation, or who consumes a vata-aggravating diet, or who drinks cold water excessively, or who suppresses the natural urges of flatus, urine, and stool, or who overeats, or who drinks unboiled new water in excessive quantities, or who is excessively agitated, or who travels by rough conveyance, or who indulges excessively in sexual activity or exercise, or who has lost his appetite, or who keeps irregular habits of eating, sleeping, sitting and walking, or engages in any other such excessive activity — from such improper conduct, vata becomes aggravated. (4)

And that vata-predominant person, especially through fever, vomiting, purgation, or diarrhea, being emaciated, the thin person of vata nature —

( 330 )

[Chapter on Gulma — Vata Gulma]

One who eats excessively cold food, or eats especially too much, or eats without prior oleation (snehana), or performs emesis and purgation, or suppresses the urges of flatus, urine, and feces after they have become enlarged; or who drinks water immediately after heavy eating, or drinks too much fresh water, or rides in vehicles while greatly agitated, or has excessive sexual activity, or has a fondness for excessive exercise and alcohol, or seeks out physical trauma, or habitually uses improper seats, beds, places of dwelling, and walking habits — or who in any such similar manner undertakes excessive exertion and the like — through such misbehavior, vata (wind-humor) becomes enraged. ॥7॥

[Sanskrit verse 5:]
The greatly aggravated vata enters the great channels, and by drying and hardening them quickly, causes a stationary mass to form. It gives rise to a gross growth in the region of the heart, the bladder, the flanks, and the navel. It generates many kinds of pain arising from vata, as well as many kinds of nodes. Since it settles and remains as a mass (pinda), and because of its mass-like nature, it is called Gulma. ॥5॥

[Prose commentary on verse 5:]
The aggravated vata, entering the channels one after another, drying and hardening them, quickly consolidates into a mass and remains fixed. It produces colic in the heart, bladder, flanks, and navel, and causes various vata-born pains.

[Sanskrit verse 6 — symptoms of Vata Gulma:]
It repeatedly grows large and then subsides to a small size. Due to the irregular nature of the pain and the mobility of vata, there is a pricking and throbbing sensation as if scattered with ants; there is stretching, contraction, exhilaration, dissolution, and rising of the mass repeatedly. The patient at that time feels as though pierced by a needle or a stake. Toward the end of the day, the mouth becomes dry, breathing is obstructed, the body hair stands on end, and with the onset of pain there is rumbling in the bowels, flatulence, intestinal gurgling, indigestion, reverse peristalsis (udavarta), body ache, stiffness of the neck, headache, pain in the temple and conch regions, and diseases of the scrotum — these complications beset him. The skin, nails, and eyes become dark, reddish, and rough, and the urine and feces likewise become so. He does not find relief in any of the postures prescribed for him, but finds relief in postures contrary to those — this is Vata Gulma. ॥6॥

[Prose commentary on verse 6:]
The mass repeatedly grows larger and then becomes smaller. Due to the irregularity of the pain and the restlessness of vata, sensations like that of ants crawling — pricking, throbbing, stretching, contraction, elation, dissolution, and rising — become more intense. At that time the patient feels as though his body is pierced by needles and stakes; and toward the end of the day...

[Page 331 — Nidanasthana, Chapter on Gulma (Abdominal Tumors/Masses)]

[Concluding description of Vata-Gulma, verse 6:]
When fever arises, the mouth becomes dry, upward movement of breath is obstructed, there is horripilation and pain in the spleen, distension of the abdomen, rumbling in the intestines, indigestion, upward movement of wind, body-ache, pain in the neck, head and temples, and scrotal disease — all these complications arise. The skin, nails, eyes, mouth, urine and stool become dark, reddish and rough. The signs mentioned in the nidana (etiology) are absent, and opposite signs appear. Thus ends the description of Vata-Gulma. ॥6॥

[Verse 7 — Sanskrit:]
By those very depleting factors affecting a person — through use of sour, salty, pungent, alkaline, hot, sharp and dry substances, spoiled wine, unripe fruits, sour and burning foods, unwholesome vegetables and meats — indigestion, overeating, and dryness follow. When these affect the stomach repeatedly, combined with excessive vomiting, purgation, suppression of natural urges, exposure to wind and sun — Vayu, along with Pitta, becomes aggravated. ॥7॥

[Prose commentary on verse 7:]
In a person already depleted by those very emaciation-causing factors, the use of sour, salty, pungent, alkaline, hot, sharp, dry, spoiled wines, unripe fruits, and sour burning things — and of those vegetables and meats that are burning — along with indigestion, overeating, and dryness — when these afflict the stomach, repeated vomiting and purgation, excessive suppression of natural urges, and overexposure to wind and sun cause Vayu together with Pitta to become inflamed. ॥7॥

[Then the aggravated Vayu, collected in one part of the stomach —]

[Sanskrit verse 8 and commentary — Pitta-Gulma:]
— produces all those varieties of pain described under Vata-Gulma. Pitta burns the region of the flanks, heart, chest or throat; the patient belches as if emitting smoke; the gulma (mass) becomes associated with acidity, burning, trembling, warmth, sweating, and moistness; it cannot bear touch and feels soft and loose; there is slight horripilation. Fever, giddiness, distress, thirst, dryness of throat and mouth, fainting, and loose stools all arise. The skin, nails, eyes, face, urine and stool become greenish-yellow. The etiological signs mentioned do not appear; the opposite signs appear and provide relief. Thus ends the description of Pitta-Gulma. ॥8॥

[Prose commentary:]
The aggravated Vayu, gathered into one region of the stomach, produces the same varieties of pain as described for Vata-Gulma. Pitta burns the flanks, heart, chest or throat; burning occurs and the patient belches as though emitting smoke, mixed with acidity. The site of the gulma becomes burning, trembling, warm, sweating and moist; it cannot bear a touch like that of something soft and loose; there is mild horripilation; fever, giddiness, distress, thirst, dryness of the throat and mouth, fainting, and passage of broken stools all occur. The skin, nails —

In the eyes, mouth, urine, and stool these changes occur, and the signs mentioned in the nidana (etiology) are not found here; rather, the opposite signs are present. Thus ends the description of pittaja gulma (bile-origin abdominal tumor). ॥8॥

When a person has been weakened by those same debilitating factors and then overeats, or consumes unctuous, heavy, sweet, and cold foods, or takes excessive preparations of ground grains, milk, black gram, sesame, molasses, and their derivatives, or drinks alcohol, or is excessively attached to sour substances, or overindulges in meats of marshy or aquatic animals, or habitually suppresses natural urges, or after being very well-nourished drinks extremely thick fluids, or is greatly agitated — through all these causes the kapha (phlegm) of the body, together with the vata (wind), becomes provoked. ॥9॥

When that provoked vata collects the kapha in one part of the stomach and thereby produces all the varieties of pain that were described under vataja gulma — the kapha also causes cold fever, loss of appetite, impaired digestion, body aches, excitement, heart disease, vomiting, excessive sleep, lethargy, heaviness, pallor, and a burning sensation in the head. ॥10॥

Furthermore —

The provoked kapha, gathered by the vata in one region, produces the same kinds of pain as described for vataja gulma; and its kaphaja characteristics cause cold fever, anorexia, indigestion, bodily pain, elation, cardiac distress, vomiting, sleepiness, laziness, stiffness, heaviness, and a burning sensation in the head. ॥10॥

The kaphaja gulma produces firmness, heaviness, hardness, and excessive numbness, as well as cough, dyspnea, catarrh, and pulmonary consumption (rajayakshma); and an extreme whitish discoloration appears in the skin, nails, eyes, face, urine, and stool. The symptoms described in the nidana section do not subside with treatments contrary to those causes; rather, they subside with treatments directed against those causes. This is the kaphaja gulma. Knowledgeable physicians describe the gulma arising from all three doshas combined (sannipataja gulma) with the signs and causes of all three. That accumulated gulma is incurable because the treatment for one dosha is contraindicated by another. ॥11॥

And the gulma — with its firmness, heaviness, hardness, and excessive numbness — similarly produces cough, dyspnea, catarrhal conditions, and pulmonary tuberculosis, as well as greatly increased pallor manifest in the skin, nails, eyes, face, urine, and stool —

[The physician] performs [treatment], and what is stated in the etiology is not present here, and [the symptoms] are opposite to those. Thus the gulma [abdominal tumor] arising from the tridosha: from the combination of signs of the three doshas, the knowledgeable physician calls it sannipata-gulma; it is treatable by prohibited measures and is called nicaya-gulma. (11)

The shonita-gulma [blood tumor] occurs only in women, not in men, because of the special nature of the uterine cavity and the blood. (12)

The shonita-gulma occurs only in women on account of the special feature of the flow of menstrual blood into the uterine cavity, and not in men. (12)

Due to dependence [on others], lack of skill, constant suppression of the urges that have arisen from continuous improper treatment — whether in the case of an early pregnancy or even a recently delivered woman — by using substances that aggravate vata during the season, vata becomes aggravated. That aggravated [vata], entering through the mouth of the vagina, obstructs the menstrual flow, and month by month as the menstrual blood is obstructed, it causes the abdomen to enlarge. (13)(14)

Due to dependence [on others] and incompetence (carelessness), by continuously suppressing the natural urges through improper conduct, when an immature fetus is partly expelled, or in the case of a woman who delivered long ago, when vata is aggravated in the menstrual season by using the substances mentioned in the verses, [the vata] becomes aggravated. That aggravated [vata], entering the mouth of the vagina, obstructs the menstrual flow; month by month the retained menstrual blood enlarges the abdomen. (13)(14)

In that woman, colic pain, cough, diarrhea, vomiting, loss of appetite, indigestion, body aches, drowsiness, lethargy, and excessive salivation arise; in the breasts there is milk, the nipples and the areolae become darkened; in the eyes there is lassitude, fainting, palpitations; in the longings [douhada] there is swelling; in the feet there is slight [swelling]; the line of hair [on the abdomen] disappears; at the entrance of the vagina there is foul smell and discharge; only the [false] tumor moves — the foolish call her a pregnant woman carrying a child in the womb. (15)(16)

Now, the preliminary signs and the manifestations of these five types of gulma [are as follows]...

Thus: — [The forerunners of gulma are:] lack of desire for food, loss of appetite, indigestion, irregularity of digestive fire, burning sensation, disturbance at the time of digestion of food, and from improper channels — obstruction of the urges of wind, urine, and stool, and even when they arise, their incomplete passage and partial obstruction; slight onset of wind-colic, distension, gurgling of the intestines, hardness of stool, absence of satisfaction in the bowels, roundness and hardness of stool, hunger, weakness, and inability to tolerate a collection [of food in the abdomen] — these are the prodromal signs of gulma. ॥ 17 ॥

In all five types of gulma, not one arises without vata [wind]. Knowing that the one arising from sannipata (combination of all three doshas) is incurable, one should not begin treatment for it. For one arising from a single dosha, treatment should be initiated according to its nature. For those arising from combined doshas, treatment should be carried out with general therapeutic measures. ॥ 18 ॥

Or if one considers anything else to be non-contradictory, one should administer that too — but only after assessing the severity and mildness of the complications. One should treat the severe complications with urgency; for the others, after observing the minor distinctions without haste. In gulma cases requiring urgent intervention, the treatment prescribed for vata should be applied. ॥ 19 ॥

And whatever one else may consider non-contradictory should also be applied after examining the severity and mildness of the complications. The severe complications should be treated quickly; in the others, one should proceed after observing minor distinctions; and in all gulma conditions, the treatment of vata must be carried out as the essential therapeutic measure. ॥ 19 ॥

Sneha (oleation) and sveda (fomentation) are the two vata-removing measures. One should administer mild purgation combined with oleation. In basti (enema), one should introduce sour, salty, and sweet-tasting substances in appropriate combination. When vata is pacified, even with little effort it becomes possible to control the other doshas as well in gulma conditions. ॥ 20 ॥
